lecture: CBL Week 3: Male Lower GU Tract and Prostate

questions.question: A 41-year-old man has sudden, colicky left flank pain that radiates to the groin and microscopic hematuria. Noncontrast CT shows a 6-mm calcified stone in the left ureter at the point where the ureter crosses the external iliac vessels, with mild hydroureter above it. At which anatomic narrowing of the ureter has the stone lodged?

explanations.A: The internal urethral orifice is the bladder outlet into the urethra, not part of the ureter.
explanations.B: The membranous urethra lies within the external urethral sphincter below the prostate and does not carry urine from the kidney.
explanations.C: The ureter narrows where it crosses the pelvic brim over the external iliac vessels, one of its three classic constriction sites.
explanations.D: The ureteropelvic junction is at the renal hilum where the pelvis becomes the ureter, well above the pelvic brim.
explanations.E: The ureterovesical junction is where the ureter passes obliquely through the bladder wall, distal to the iliac vessel crossing.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man has a large central L5–S1 disc herniation compressing the cauda equina. He reports saddle anesthesia and has not voided for 14 hours. Bladder scan shows 950 mL of urine, and he has no urge to void. Loss of which nerve fibers best explains his inability to empty the bladder?

answers.B: Inferior rectal branches of the pudendal nerve

explanations.A: The dorsal nerve of the penis carries sensation from the penis and has no role in detrusor contraction.
explanations.B: The inferior rectal nerve supplies the external anal sphincter and perianal skin, not the detrusor.
explanations.C: Least thoracic splanchnic fibers are sympathetic fibers mainly to the kidney and upper ureter, not motor to the detrusor.
explanations.D: Sympathetic T11–L2 fibers contract the internal urethral sphincter during storage; losing them would favor leakage, not retention.
explanations.E: Parasympathetic S2–S4 fibers in the pelvic splanchnic nerves contract the detrusor and relax the internal sphincter, so their loss causes painless retention.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man undergoes open radical prostatectomy. While dissecting along the lateral pelvic wall toward the base of the bladder, the surgeon identifies a firm cord that passes from the deep inguinal ring, crosses the external iliac vessels, and then runs superior to (over) the ureter before joining the duct of the seminal vesicle. Which structure is this?

explanations.A: The ductus deferens leaves the deep inguinal ring, crosses the external iliac vessels, passes over the ureter, and joins the seminal vesicle duct to form the ejaculatory duct.
explanations.B: The inferior vesical artery arises from the internal iliac and runs medially to the bladder base and prostate; it does not come from the inguinal ring.
explanations.C: The obturator nerve runs along the lateral pelvic wall to the obturator foramen and does not join the seminal vesicle.
explanations.D: The pudendal nerve leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and runs in the pudendal canal to the perineum.
explanations.E: The superior vesical artery comes from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery and supplies the upper bladder and distal ureter.

questions.question: A 27-year-old man is brought in after a motorcycle crash with a pelvic fracture involving the pubic rami. He has blood at the urethral meatus, cannot void, and on rectal exam the prostate is high-riding. Retrograde urethrogram shows contrast leaking just below the apex of the prostate. Which part of the urethra is most likely injured?

explanations.A: The intramural (preprostatic) urethra lies in the bladder neck, above the prostate, not below its apex.
explanations.B: The membranous urethra runs from the prostatic apex to the bulb of the penis through the external urethral sphincter and is the part torn in pelvic fractures.
explanations.C: The navicular fossa is the distal dilation of the spongy urethra in the glans, far from the prostatic apex.
explanations.D: The prostatic urethra lies inside the prostate, with the urethral crest and ejaculatory duct openings, above the injury shown.
explanations.E: The spongy urethra lies in the corpus spongiosum and is classically injured by straddle injuries, not pelvic fractures.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man has a testicular biopsy as part of an infertility workup. A section taken between the rete testis and the head of the epididymis shows the duct below: the lining alternates between tall and short columnar cells, giving a wavy luminal border, and the duct is wrapped by a thin layer of smooth muscle. Which structure is shown?

explanations.A: Efferent ductules connect the rete testis to the epididymis and have a scalloped lining of alternating tall and short columnar cells.
explanations.B: The epididymal duct has very uniform, tall pseudostratified columnar cells with stereocilia and a smooth luminal border.
explanations.C: The rete testis is a network of channels lined by simple cuboidal epithelium within the mediastinum testis.
explanations.D: Seminiferous tubules contain Sertoli cells and layers of developing germ cells, not a simple ductal lining.
explanations.E: Straight tubules (tubuli recti) connect the seminiferous tubules to the rete testis and are lined by simple cuboidal epithelium.

questions.question: A researcher tracks a fluorescently tagged androgen receptor in cultured prostate stromal cells. In androgen-free medium, most of the signal is cytoplasmic. Within minutes of adding DHT, the signal moves into the nucleus. Release from which bound protein is required for this movement?

explanations.A: Androgen-binding protein is secreted by Sertoli cells to keep local androgen levels high in the seminiferous tubules; it does not hold AR in the cytoplasm.
explanations.B: Unliganded AR sits in the cytoplasm bound to chaperones, especially HSP90; DHT binding causes a conformational change that releases them so AR can enter the nucleus.
explanations.C: SHBG carries testosterone in the plasma and is outside the cell, not bound to intracellular AR.
explanations.D: Src takes part in rapid non-genomic AR signaling as a co-activator; it does not hold AR in the cytoplasm.
explanations.E: StAR moves cholesterol into mitochondria for steroid synthesis in Leydig cells and does not bind AR.

questions.question: A 17-year-old phenotypic female (46,XY) has primary amenorrhea, scant pubic and axillary hair, a blind vaginal pouch, and inguinal testes. Testosterone and LH are elevated. Genetic testing shows an X-linked androgen receptor mutation; in vitro, the mutant receptor binds DHT normally and enters the nucleus but cannot activate androgen-responsive genes. Which receptor region is most likely mutated?

explanations.A: A ligand-binding domain defect would stop DHT from binding, but this receptor binds DHT normally.
explanations.B: The hinge region is a flexible linker that helps nuclear transport, so its loss would impair nuclear entry, which is normal here.
explanations.C: AR is an intracellular nuclear receptor with no membrane-spanning segment.
explanations.D: AR is a type 1 nuclear hormone receptor, not a receptor tyrosine kinase, and has no kinase domain.
explanations.E: The DNA-binding domain uses two zinc fingers to recognize androgen response elements, so a defect there allows ligand binding and nuclear entry but no transcription.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man treated with chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma 3 years ago is evaluated for infertility. He has normal libido, erections, muscle mass, and body hair. Semen analysis shows azoospermia. Laboratory results are shown. Loss of which product of the damaged cell type best explains the hormone pattern?

explanations.A: AMH from Sertoli cells regresses Müllerian ducts in the fetus and does not feed back on pituitary FSH.
explanations.B: Estradiol from aromatized testosterone feeds back on both LH and FSH, and his normal testosterone means estradiol should be normal.
explanations.C: GnRH is a hypothalamic hormone; low GnRH would lower both LH and FSH rather than raise FSH alone.
explanations.D: Sertoli cells (driven by FSH) secrete inhibin B, which selectively suppresses FSH; Sertoli damage drops inhibin B and isolates an FSH rise while Leydig function stays normal.
explanations.E: Leydig-cell testosterone suppresses both LH and FSH; here testosterone and LH are normal, so Leydig cells are intact.

questions.question: A 29-year-old competitive bodybuilder presents with 1 year of infertility. He has acne, increased muscle mass, and bilaterally small, soft testes. Semen analysis shows azoospermia. Laboratory results are shown. Which mechanism best explains his azoospermia?

answers.A: Androgen receptor downregulation in skeletal muscle
answers.B: Obstruction of the ductus deferens by fibrosis
answers.C: Primary Leydig cell failure from direct androgen toxicity
answers.D: Sertoli cell destruction causing low inhibin B

explanations.A: His muscle has clearly responded to androgen, and muscle AR status does not control spermatogenesis.
explanations.B: Obstruction causes azoospermia with normal testis size and normal gonadotropins, not small testes and suppressed LH and FSH.
explanations.C: Primary Leydig failure would raise LH through lost feedback, but his LH is suppressed.
explanations.D: Sertoli destruction would remove inhibin B feedback and raise FSH, but his FSH is suppressed.
explanations.E: Exogenous androgen suppresses GnRH, LH, and FSH, so Leydig cells stop making the high local testosterone that Sertoli cells need for spermatogenesis.

questions.question: A newborn with a 46,XY karyotype has ambiguous external genitalia, with a small phallus, a bifid scrotum, and perineal hypospadias. Testes are palpable in the labioscrotal folds. Imaging shows an epididymis, ductus deferens, and seminal vesicles on both sides and no uterus. Serum testosterone is normal for age, with a high testosterone-to-DHT ratio. Which hormones are required for his internal ducts and for his external genitalia, respectively?

explanations.A: AMH regresses the Müllerian ducts (explaining no uterus) but does not form Wolffian structures, and estradiol does not masculinize the genitalia.
explanations.B: This reverses the roles: Wolffian ducts depend on testosterone and the external genitalia on DHT.
explanations.C: Estradiol does not preserve the Wolffian ducts; testosterone does.
explanations.D: Inhibin B suppresses FSH and has no role in forming the internal ducts, and the external genitalia need DHT.
explanations.E: Testosterone alone preserves the Wolffian ducts (epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicles), but DHT made by 5α-reductase is needed to masculinize the external genitalia.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is started on hCG injections, which act on the LH receptor. Within hours, Leydig-cell testosterone output rises. The earliest regulated step in this response depends on which protein?

explanations.A: 17β-HSD converts androstenedione to testosterone late in the pathway, not the earliest regulated step.
explanations.B: 5α-reductase converts testosterone to DHT in target tissues like the prostate, after testosterone is made.
explanations.C: Aromatase converts testosterone to estradiol and acts after testosterone synthesis.
explanations.D: Cytochrome b5 boosts the 17,20-lyase activity of CYP17 at a middle step, not the earliest regulated one.
explanations.E: LH/hCG signaling through cAMP rapidly increases StAR, which moves cholesterol into the mitochondria for CYP11A1 cleavage, the regulated first step of steroid synthesis.

questions.question: A 71-year-old man has 3 years of a weak urinary stream, hesitancy, straining, and getting up three times a night to void. On digital rectal exam the prostate is symmetrically enlarged, smooth, rubbery, and nontender, with no discrete nodules. Postvoid residual is 180 mL. In which region of the prostate does the process causing his symptoms most likely arise?

explanations.A: The anterior fibromuscular stroma is non-glandular and is not the usual source of hyperplastic nodules.
explanations.B: The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and is an uncommon site for both BPH and carcinoma.
explanations.C: The peripheral zone is the usual site of adenocarcinoma, which is far from the urethra and usually palpable as a hard nodule.
explanations.D: The seminal vesicles are separate glands posterior to the bladder, not part of the prostate's zones.
explanations.E: BPH arises as nodules in the transition zone and periurethral tissue, so it compresses the prostatic urethra and causes obstructive symptoms early.

explanationImage.caption: Cut surface of an enlarged prostate

questions.question: A 64-year-old man has a PSA that has risen from 3.1 to 6.8 ng/mL over 2 years and a firm area at the left base of the prostate on rectal exam. A core from that area shows small, crowded glands lined by a single layer of cells with enlarged nuclei and prominent nucleoli, shown below. Which immunohistochemical result would confirm the most likely diagnosis?

answers.A: AMACR negative, basal cell markers positive
answers.B: AMACR positive, basal cell markers negative
answers.C: AMACR positive, basal cell markers positive

explanations.A: This is the pattern of benign glands, including BPH, which keep their basal cells and lack AMACR.
explanations.B: Adenocarcinoma overexpresses AMACR (p504s) and has lost its basal cell layer, so basal markers like p63 and high-molecular-weight keratin are negative.
explanations.C: AMACR positivity with retained basal cells indicates high-grade PIN, a precursor that has not invaded.
explanations.D: Prostatic adenocarcinoma usually keeps AR and PSA expression, which is why it responds to androgen deprivation.
explanations.E: This pattern suggests a mesenchymal tumor such as a sarcoma, not a gland-forming carcinoma.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man has 2 months of worsening low back pain that wakes him at night. He has not seen a physician in 15 years. Rectal exam shows a hard, irregular, nontender nodule in the prostate. Laboratory results are shown. Spine radiographs are most likely to show which finding?

answers.A: Dense sclerotic lesions in the vertebral bodies
answers.C: Expansile lytic lesion with a soap-bubble pattern
answers.E: Vertebral disc space narrowing with endplate erosion

explanations.A: Prostate cancer spreads to the axial skeleton and classically forms osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions, which raise alkaline phosphatase.
explanations.B: Punched-out lytic lesions with normal ALP are typical of multiple myeloma, not prostate cancer.
explanations.C: A soap-bubble lytic lesion suggests giant cell tumor or renal cell metastasis, not prostate cancer.
explanations.D: Diffuse osteopenia suggests osteoporosis, which would not raise PSA or ALP this much.
explanations.E: Disc space loss with endplate destruction suggests discitis-osteomyelitis, which crosses the disc, unlike metastases.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man has a 12-core prostate biopsy for a PSA of 9.2 ng/mL. The tumor is mostly made of the pattern shown below: glands fused into large back-to-back sheets with multiple small, punched-out, sieve-like lumens. Which Gleason pattern does this architecture represent?

explanations.A: Patterns 1–2 are well-formed, uniform, closely packed glands and are rarely assigned in modern practice.
explanations.B: Pattern 2 is also well-formed uniform glands and would not show fused cribriform sheets.
explanations.C: Pattern 3 is discrete, separate infiltrating glands with stroma between them, not fused glands.
explanations.D: Fused, poorly formed, and cribriform (sieve-like) glands define Gleason pattern 4, which moves a tumor out of Grade Group 1.
explanations.E: Pattern 5 has no gland formation: solid sheets, cords, single cells, or comedonecrosis.

questions.question: A 63-year-old man with a life expectancy of more than 15 years has a nonpalpable prostate cancer found on biopsy for a PSA of 7.5 ng/mL. Pathology shows Gleason 4 + 3 = 7 in 5 of 12 cores. MRI shows no extraprostatic extension. What is the most appropriate management?

answers.A: Active surveillance with PSA every 6 months

explanations.A: Active surveillance is for very-low and low risk (GG1) and selected favorable intermediate (limited GG2), not GG3.
explanations.B: ADT alone is not curative for localized disease in a healthy man; it is used with radiation or for advanced disease.
explanations.C: Gleason 4 + 3 is Grade Group 3 (unfavorable intermediate risk), which is clinically significant and warrants definitive treatment.
explanations.D: Delaying treatment with interval biopsy is part of active surveillance, which is inappropriate for GG3.
explanations.E: Watchful waiting has no curative intent and is for men with a life expectancy of 5 years or less.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man has 2 days of fever to 39.4°C, chills, perineal pain, dysuria, and urinary urgency. Pulse is 112/min. A gentle rectal exam shows a warm, swollen, boggy, and exquisitely tender prostate. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. What is the most likely causative organism?

explanations.A: Chlamydia causes urethritis and epididymitis in young men but is not the main cause of acute bacterial prostatitis with sepsis.
explanations.B: Enterococcus is a larger share of chronic bacterial prostatitis and catheter-related infections than of acute prostatitis.
explanations.C: E. coli, a lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod with fimbriae, causes most acute bacterial prostatitis, usually by ascending infection from the urethra.
explanations.D: Pseudomonas mostly causes healthcare- and catheter-associated infections, not community acute prostatitis.
explanations.E: S. saprophyticus causes UTIs mainly in sexually active young women and is a rare cause of prostatitis.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man has had three episodes of E. coli cystitis in 9 months, each with the same susceptibility pattern. Between episodes he has mild perineal discomfort. A four-glass (Meares–Stamey) test grows E. coli only in the expressed prostatic secretions and the post-massage urine. He is started on a 6-week course of levofloxacin instead of nitrofurantoin. Which property of levofloxacin best explains this choice?

answers.B: High concentration in bladder urine only
answers.C: Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis

explanations.A: The organism is a gram-negative rod, and gram-positive coverage does not explain the drug choice.
explanations.B: Drugs like nitrofurantoin concentrate in urine but do not reach prostatic tissue, which is why they fail in prostatitis.
explanations.C: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV, not cell wall synthesis.
explanations.D: Chronic bacterial prostatitis needs a lipid-soluble drug such as a fluoroquinolone to cross the prostatic barrier and reach bacteria in fibrotic tissue and biofilm.
explanations.E: Urease matters for Proteus and struvite stones and is not a property of levofloxacin.

questions.question: A 33-year-old man has 8 months of aching pain in the perineum, testicles, and lower abdomen, with painful ejaculation and mild urinary frequency. He has never had fever. Rectal exam shows a normal-sized, mildly tender prostate. Urinalysis is normal, and cultures of urine and expressed prostatic secretions are repeatedly negative. Which mechanism best explains his ongoing pain?

answers.A: Biofilm-protected bacteria in fibrotic prostate tissue
answers.B: Central sensitization after an inflammatory trigger
answers.C: Compression of the prostatic urethra by transition-zone nodules
answers.E: Prostatic abscess formation from ascending infection

explanations.A: Biofilm and fibrosis explain chronic bacterial prostatitis, which causes recurrent UTIs with positive cultures.
explanations.B: Chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome has no infection and is thought to follow a trigger that leads to immune activation and central sensitization.
explanations.C: Transition-zone nodules are BPH, which causes obstructive symptoms in older men, not chronic pelvic pain with negative cultures.
explanations.D: Prostate cancer is usually painless locally, rare at 33, and would not explain this pain syndrome.
explanations.E: A prostatic abscess follows acute bacterial prostatitis with fever and sepsis, not afebrile pain with negative cultures.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man with a long-term indwelling urethral catheter for urinary retention has foul-smelling urine and low-grade fever. CT shows a large branching calculus filling the right renal pelvis. Laboratory results are shown. Which virulence factor of the most likely organism explains the stone?
table: Motile gram-negative rod with swarming growth

explanations.A: Fimbriae let E. coli attach to urothelium and resist being flushed out, but they do not alkalinize urine or form stones.
explanations.B: Lipoteichoic acid is a component of gram-positive cell walls and does not cause struvite stones.
explanations.C: The capsule of Klebsiella resists phagocytosis but does not raise urine pH.
explanations.D: Proteus mirabilis urease splits urea into ammonia, alkalinizing the urine and precipitating magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) stones.
explanations.E: Vancomycin resistance matters for Enterococcus treatment and has no role in stone formation.

questions.question: A 77-year-old man had an indwelling urinary catheter placed 10 days ago for acute urinary retention from BPH and was treated with ceftriaxone for a presumed UTI. He now has fever and cloudy urine. Urine culture grows gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains that are catalase-negative and grow in 6.5% NaCl and bile esculin. Which organism is most likely?

explanations.A: Enterococcus is a catalase-negative gram-positive coccus in pairs and chains, causes catheter-associated UTIs, and is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins.
explanations.B: Klebsiella is an encapsulated, lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod.
explanations.C: Proteus is a motile gram-negative rod with urease, not a gram-positive coccus.
explanations.D: S. saprophyticus forms clusters, is catalase-positive and novobiocin-resistant, and mainly causes UTIs in young women.
explanations.E: Group B strep is a catalase-negative coccus in chains but is CAMP-positive and hippurate-positive, not bile esculin-positive or salt-tolerant.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man asks about prostate cancer screening. He feels well and has no urinary symptoms. He recently learned he carries a pathogenic germline BRCA2 variant after his sister was diagnosed with breast cancer. Which screening plan is most appropriate?

answers.B: Begin PSA testing at age 45 every 2–4 years
answers.C: Begin PSA testing at age 50 if symptoms develop
answers.D: Defer screening until a first-degree male relative is diagnosed
answers.E: Obtain prostate MRI every year instead of PSA

explanations.A: Germline BRCA2 carriers have a higher risk of aggressive cancer at a younger age, so systematic annual PSA from age 40 is recommended.
explanations.B: Starting at 45 applies to average-risk men; his BRCA2 variant moves him to the higher-risk pathway beginning at 40.
explanations.C: Waiting for symptoms defeats screening, and prostate cancer is usually asymptomatic early.
explanations.D: His germline variant already confers higher risk without needing an affected male relative.
explanations.E: MRI is used to evaluate an abnormal PSA or during surveillance, not as the first screening test.

questions.question: A 79-year-old man with long-standing weak stream, nocturia, and incomplete emptying has had 3 days of overflow dribbling and lower abdominal fullness. On exam the bladder is palpable to the umbilicus and the prostate is smooth, symmetrically enlarged, and nontender. Laboratory results are shown. Ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis and a thick, trabeculated bladder wall. Which mechanism best explains his kidney injury?

answers.A: Acute tubular necrosis from nephrotoxic drugs
answers.C: Bilateral ureteral invasion by prostatic carcinoma
answers.D: Prerenal hypoperfusion from poor oral intake

explanations.A: ATN is an intrinsic renal injury and does not cause hydronephrosis or a bladder distended to the umbilicus.
explanations.B: BPH nodules compress the prostatic urethra; retained urine raises pressure in the bladder and both ureters, causing hydronephrosis and postrenal AKI.
explanations.C: His smooth, symmetric, nontender prostate points to BPH, and carcinoma rarely invades both ureters.
explanations.D: Prerenal AKI does not cause bilateral hydronephrosis or a distended bladder.
explanations.E: Retroperitoneal fibrosis causes bilateral hydronephrosis but with a normal, non-distended bladder.

questions.question: A 72-year-old man has received leuprolide for 3 years for biochemically recurrent prostate cancer. He now has hot flashes, reduced libido, breast tenderness, and a new vertebral compression fracture after minor trauma. DEXA shows a T-score of −2.8 at the lumbar spine. Loss of which hormone action most directly explains his bone loss?

explanations.A: DHT drives prostate growth, body hair, and sebum; it is not the main hormone protecting male bone density.
explanations.B: Testosterone is aromatized to estradiol, which limits bone resorption; ADT removes testosterone and therefore estradiol, accelerating bone loss.
explanations.C: Inhibin B is a Sertoli-cell product that suppresses FSH and is not the main protector of bone.
explanations.D: LH acts on Leydig cells to make testosterone and does not act directly on bone.
explanations.E: Testosterone does not directly regulate PTH; the bone effect comes mainly through its conversion to estradiol.

questions.question: A community clinic screens 1000 men aged 55–69 for prostate cancer with PSA (cutoff 4.0 ng/mL), and all men then undergo biopsy. The results are shown. A 62-year-old man from this group has a PSA of 5.1 ng/mL and asks how likely it is that he has cancer. What is the best estimate?

explanations.A: 10% is the overall prevalence of cancer (100 of 1000), not the probability given a positive test.
explanations.B: PPV = true positives / all positives = 30 / (30 + 90) = 25%, typical for a PSA of 4–10.
explanations.C: 30% is the sensitivity, 30 / (30 + 70), the share of men with cancer who test positive.
explanations.D: 90% is the specificity, 810 / (810 + 90), the share of men without cancer who test negative.
explanations.E: 92% is the negative predictive value, 810 / (810 + 70), which applies to a negative result.

questions.question: A PSA cutoff of 4.0 ng/mL has a fixed sensitivity and specificity. The same test is applied in two clinics: one serves average-risk men, and the other serves Black men aged 60–70 who each have two first-degree relatives with prostate cancer. Compared with the average-risk clinic, how will a positive result in the high-risk clinic differ?

explanations.A: Higher prevalence lowers NPV because more negative results are false negatives.
explanations.B: Sensitivity and specificity do not change with prevalence, but higher prevalence raises the PPV of a positive result and lowers the NPV.
explanations.C: Sensitivity is fixed by the test and cutoff and does not depend on the population screened.
explanations.D: Specificity is a property of the test and cutoff and does not change with prevalence.
explanations.E: PPV falls when prevalence falls, not when it rises.

questions.question: A 61-year-old man with biopsy-proven prostate cancer has a staging sagittal T2-weighted pelvic MRI. The radiologist reports tumor extending from the prostate base into the paired, lobulated glands that lie posterior to the bladder base, superior to the prostate, and anterior to the rectum. Which structure is involved, and what pathologic T stage would this correspond to if confirmed at surgery?

explanations.A: Bladder neck invasion is pT3a, but the bladder neck is the bladder outlet just above the prostate, not paired posterior glands.
explanations.B: The bulbourethral glands are small glands beside the membranous urethra, below the prostate.
explanations.C: The ductus deferens joins the seminal vesicle duct, but pT2 means organ-confined disease, which this is not.
explanations.D: The mesorectum surrounds the rectum; invasion of the rectum or pelvic wall is pT4.
explanations.E: The seminal vesicles sit behind the bladder base, above the prostate and in front of the rectum, and seminal vesicle invasion is pT3b.

explanationImage.caption: Sagittal T2-weighted MRI of the male pelvis, labelled

questions.question: A 67-year-old man who has smoked 1 pack per day for 45 years notices bright red urine with small clots on three occasions over the past month. He has no pain, fever, or dysuria, and urinary stream is normal. Urinalysis confirms red blood cells without casts or protein, and urine culture is negative. Which next step is most appropriate?

explanations.A: Painless gross hematuria in an older smoker is urothelial carcinoma until proven otherwise; cystoscopy examines the bladder and CT urography the upper tracts.
explanations.B: His culture is negative and he has no infectious symptoms, so antibiotics are not indicated.
explanations.C: Kidney biopsy is for glomerular hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, or proteinuria, which he does not have.
explanations.D: PSA does not evaluate the urothelium, and BPH or prostate cancer cannot be assumed as the source of gross hematuria.
explanations.E: Gross hematuria in a high-risk patient needs prompt evaluation; waiting delays diagnosis of bladder cancer.

questions.question: A 64-year-old man in good health (life expectancy more than 15 years) has a normal rectal exam. Biopsy for an elevated PSA shows prostate adenocarcinoma. The findings are shown. He is worried about incontinence and erectile dysfunction. What is the most appropriate management?

explanations.A: Very-low-risk disease (cT1c, GG1, fewer than 3 positive cores, ≤50% per core, PSA density <0.15) is best managed by active surveillance, sparing treatment side effects.
explanations.B: ADT is for intermediate/high-risk, locally advanced, or metastatic disease, and its side effects are not justified here.
explanations.C: Radiation with ADT is for high-risk disease (GG4–5, PSA >20, or cT3 or higher).
explanations.D: Definitive surgery would overtreat an indolent GG1 tumor and risk incontinence and impotence.
explanations.E: Watchful waiting has no curative intent and is for men with a life expectancy of 5 years or less.

questions.question: An 86-year-old man with NYHA class IV heart failure, oxygen-dependent COPD, and an estimated life expectancy of under 2 years has a nonpalpable Gleason 3 + 4 = 7 prostate cancer found during a workup for anemia. He has no urinary or bone symptoms. What is the most appropriate management?

answers.A: Active surveillance with biopsy every 12 months
answers.D: Radical prostatectomy with lymph node dissection

explanations.A: Active surveillance has curative intent with scheduled biopsies and suits healthier men with a life expectancy of more than 10 years.
explanations.B: Curative radiation is not warranted when he is likely to die of something else first.
explanations.C: ADT is reserved for symptomatic progression in watchful waiting, and starting it now adds side effects without benefit.
explanations.D: Surgery carries major risk and no survival benefit given his competing illnesses.
explanations.E: With a life expectancy of 5 years or less, watchful waiting avoids curative treatment and scheduled biopsies, treating only symptoms if they arise.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man with bothersome LUTS from BPH starts a new medication. Within a week his stream is stronger and he gets up less at night. He reports lightheadedness when standing quickly and notes that he has little or no ejaculate at orgasm. Prostate volume is unchanged at 6 months. Which mechanism best explains both the benefit and the side effects?

answers.A: Antagonism of muscarinic receptors in the detrusor
answers.B: Blockade of the androgen receptor in prostate
answers.C: Blockade of α1 receptors in prostatic smooth muscle
answers.D: Inhibition of 5α-reductase type 2 in prostatic stroma

explanations.A: Antimuscarinics reduce urgency but can worsen retention and cause dry mouth, not orthostatic hypotension and dry ejaculate.
explanations.B: Antiandrogens cause gynecomastia and hot flashes and are not used for routine BPH.
explanations.C: α1 blockers like tamsulosin relax smooth muscle of the bladder neck and prostate for fast relief, and cause orthostatic hypotension and retrograde ejaculation.
explanations.D: 5-ARIs shrink the gland over 3–6 months and cause reduced libido, but they would not give relief within a week or cause orthostasis.
explanations.E: PDE5 inhibitors can ease LUTS but cause headache, flushing, and nasal congestion, not retrograde ejaculation.

questions.question: A 68-year-old man has taken finasteride for BPH for 2 years. Before he started, his PSA was 2.6 ng/mL. His PSA was 1.3 ng/mL at 1 year and is now 2.4 ng/mL. Rectal exam shows a smooth, enlarged gland. Which is the best interpretation of his current PSA?

answers.A: Expected result of continued prostate growth on finasteride
answers.B: Laboratory error because finasteride does not affect PSA
answers.C: Normal because PSA below 4 rules out cancer
answers.D: Reassuring because it is below his pretreatment value
answers.E: Suspicious rise equal to about 4.8 ng/mL off treatment

explanations.A: Finasteride shrinks the gland and lowers PSA, so a rising PSA is not expected.
explanations.B: Finasteride lowers PSA by about 50%, so a change is expected and must be accounted for.
explanations.C: No PSA level is low enough to rule out cancer, and his corrected value is about 4.8.
explanations.D: On finasteride, the PSA should stay around half the baseline; a return to near baseline is a rise, not reassurance.
explanations.E: 5-ARIs halve PSA, so his PSA should be doubled (2.4 to about 4.8); a rise after the expected nadir on finasteride warrants evaluation for cancer.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man had a radical prostatectomy for Gleason 4 + 3 = 7 cancer with negative margins 2 years ago. His PSA was undetectable at 6 weeks after surgery. Serial PSA values are now 0.12, 0.21, and 0.34 ng/mL over the past 9 months. Which is the best interpretation?

answers.B: Castration-resistant disease needing a new hormonal agent
answers.C: Expected low-level PSA from remaining normal prostate
answers.D: PSA bounce that will resolve without treatment
answers.E: Recurrence only if the PSA exceeds nadir plus 2

explanations.A: PSA should be undetectable after prostatectomy; a confirmed rise to ≥0.2 indicates residual or recurrent disease, prompting PSMA PET and salvage radiation.
explanations.B: Castration resistance means a rising PSA despite castrate testosterone on ADT, and he is not on ADT.
explanations.C: After prostatectomy no normal prostate should remain, so any rising PSA reflects cancer.
explanations.D: PSA bounce is a temporary rise after radiation, especially brachytherapy, not after prostatectomy.
explanations.E: Nadir + 2 (Phoenix) defines recurrence after radiation, not after prostatectomy.

questions.question: A 70-year-old man was treated with brachytherapy for intermediate-risk prostate cancer. His PSA fell slowly to a nadir of 0.6 ng/mL at 18 months. At 24 months it is 1.4 ng/mL, and 4 months later it is 0.9 ng/mL. He has no symptoms. Which is the best interpretation?

answers.B: Biochemical recurrence by the Phoenix definition
answers.D: Residual disease because PSA should be undetectable

explanations.A: A temporary rise 1–3 years after radiation, especially brachytherapy, that stays below nadir + 2 and then falls is a bounce, not recurrence.
explanations.B: Phoenix recurrence needs a PSA of nadir + 2 (here 2.6 ng/mL), which he never reached.
explanations.C: Castration resistance applies to men on ADT with castrate testosterone; he is not on ADT.
explanations.D: Undetectable PSA is expected after prostatectomy; after radiation the PSA falls slowly and is never zero.
explanations.E: His PSA is falling again and never met recurrence criteria, so salvage treatment is not indicated.

questions.question: A 74-year-old man with prostate cancer metastatic to the thoracic spine starts monthly leuprolide alone. Ten days later he has worsening back pain and new leg weakness. Serum testosterone has risen above his baseline. Which drug should have been started with leuprolide to prevent this?

explanations.A: GnRH agonists first stimulate LH release and cause a testosterone flare; an androgen receptor antagonist like bicalutamide blocks the flare.
explanations.B: Finasteride blocks conversion to DHT in the prostate but does not block testosterone at the receptor during a flare.
explanations.C: Sildenafil is a PDE5 inhibitor for erectile dysfunction and has no effect on testosterone signaling.
explanations.D: Tamsulosin relaxes prostatic smooth muscle for LUTS and has no antiandrogen effect.
explanations.E: Zoledronic acid reduces skeletal events from bone metastases but does not prevent the testosterone flare.

questions.question: A 69-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer on leuprolide starts an oral drug that inhibits CYP17 (17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase) in the adrenal glands, testes, and tumor. He did not take the prednisone that was prescribed with it. Three weeks later he has leg edema and muscle weakness. Laboratory results are shown. Which mechanism best explains his findings?

answers.A: Androgen receptor upregulation in renal tubules
answers.D: Gonadotropin surge from GnRH agonist flare
answers.E: Testosterone deficiency causing renal potassium loss

explanations.A: AR changes in the kidney do not cause mineralocorticoid excess or hypokalemia.
explanations.B: Aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) is not the target; aldosterone itself is often low as ACTH-driven precursors rise.
explanations.C: Blocking CYP17 lowers cortisol, so ACTH rises and drives precursors like 11-deoxycorticosterone, causing hypertension, hypokalemia, and edema; prednisone prevents this.
explanations.D: A testosterone flare causes bone pain or obstruction, not hypokalemia and hypertension.
explanations.E: Low testosterone causes hot flashes, bone loss, and metabolic changes, not renal potassium wasting.

questions.question: A 63-year-old man with stable angina who uses sublingual nitroglycerin as needed takes sildenafil he obtained from a friend. Thirty minutes later he gets chest pain, uses his nitroglycerin, and soon becomes lightheaded and collapses. Blood pressure is 68/40 mm Hg. Which mechanism best explains the interaction?

answers.A: Blockade of α1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle
answers.B: Hepatic CYP3A4 inhibition raising nitroglycerin levels
answers.C: Inhibition of PDE3 raising cardiac cAMP
answers.D: Nitrate-driven cGMP made with its breakdown blocked
answers.E: Reflex bradycardia from increased vagal tone

explanations.A: α1 blockade explains orthostasis with tamsulosin, not the sildenafil–nitrate interaction.
explanations.B: Sildenafil is metabolized by the liver but does not raise nitroglycerin levels; the interaction is pharmacodynamic.
explanations.C: PDE3 inhibitors like milrinone raise cAMP in the heart; sildenafil selectively inhibits PDE5.
explanations.D: Nitrates release NO, which raises cGMP; PDE5 inhibitors block cGMP breakdown, so together they cause profound vasodilation and hypotension.
explanations.E: The collapse is from vasodilation lowering preload and afterload, not from vagally mediated bradycardia.

questions.question: A nurse on a urology ward prepares an intravenous dose of gentamicin for a man in bed A of a shared room. The man in bed B, who has severe kidney disease and a gentamicin allergy, is about to receive it when he notices the name on the label is not his and stops the nurse. No drug is given. How should this event be classified?

explanations.A: An ameliorable adverse event is a harm that was not preventable but could have been less severe; no harm occurred here.
explanations.B: A near miss is an unsafe event identical to a preventable adverse event except that no harm occurred, here because the patient caught the error.
explanations.C: A negligent adverse event is harm from care below community standards; this patient was not harmed.
explanations.D: A nonpreventable adverse event is harm despite standard, non-negligent care; this was an error and caused no harm.
explanations.E: A preventable adverse event requires actual harm from an error; the drug was never given.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man with favorable intermediate-risk prostate cancer chooses definitive treatment and asks how the two main options differ. He says that keeping control of his bowels is most important to him because he drives a delivery truck for 10 hours a day. Which statement best compares the side effects of radical prostatectomy with those of radiation?

answers.A: Both carry the same risk of bowel symptoms
answers.B: Radiation causes stress incontinence; surgery causes proctitis
answers.C: Radiation preserves fertility; surgery spares erections
answers.D: Surgery has better cancer control at the cost of more bowel symptoms
answers.E: Surgery risks stress incontinence; radiation risks rectal injury

explanations.A: Rectal side effects such as proctitis are specific to radiation; prostatectomy rarely affects bowel function.
explanations.B: This reverses the typical pattern: surgery causes stress incontinence and radiation causes proctitis.
explanations.C: Both can cause erectile dysfunction, and surgery removes the prostate and seminal vesicles, causing permanent infertility.
explanations.D: The two have similar cancer outcomes, and surgery does not carry more bowel symptoms.
explanations.E: Prostatectomy causes permanent infertility, usually transient stress incontinence, and possible impotence, while radiation causes urgency, hematuria, and rectal side effects.
